speaker: Maitri
line: Gathak. Good — it worked. I was not sure anyone would answer.

speaker: Maitri
line: Look down. That is the Gatha: a scroll of eleven painted panels, laid out as an island. Eleven eras, side by side. Most of it is clear. Some of it is not.

speaker: Maitri
line: The grey is the Dhundh. It does one of two things to a story: gilds it into a fairy tale, or erases it into a shrug. It cannot survive one question: how do we know that?

speaker: Maitri
line: You carry three things. The bow, for what needs precision. The shilpa tools, for what was broken. And the Pramana lens. Hold right-click on anything old, and it will tell you how we know it, not just what it is.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: No need to check. Just enjoy the view.

speaker: Maitri
line: Do not listen to that. Land.

speaker: Maitri
line: Look how clear the air is. Nobody here left anything we can read, so the Dhundh has nothing to gild or erase. It just waits.

speaker: Maitri
line: Start with the ground. Hold the lens on what you find, and ask of everything: how do we know that?

speaker: Ekarupa
line: No writing, no names, no kings. What is there to know? Enjoy the view, and leave it at that.

speaker: Maitri
line: You chose the oldest panel to begin with. Good. Everything else on this island learns its habits from here.

speaker: Maitri
line: Hemaka sows into the mud the flood leaves behind, and cotton leaves the field as raw fibre. Follow it to the weaver in the lower town: Sujata.

speaker: Maitri
line: Spun, woven, dyed with madder — and not made for the city. Cloth like this goes out in bales. Take it down to the dock, to Kaushi.

speaker: Maitri
line: Follow the cloth and you have followed the whole economy: field, loom, quay, boat. Every handover was a trade, and every trade needed a weight both sides trusted. Hold that thought. The next place is where somebody wrote it all down.

speaker: Bhadra
line: You set the slabs back in the right order. That is the whole secret of this city, you know. Not the Great Bath. The people who lift the slabs.

speaker: Ashvini
line: Thirty-two units, no more, no less. The same weights turn up in towns a long walk apart. Somebody agreed on that, and kept agreeing.

speaker: Maitri
line: That is the first panel mended. Look at what it shows: a seal pressed into red clay, an animal and a short row of signs — and underneath, one line left blank. Unread. I could paint a reading into it. People have, for a century.

speaker: Maitri
line: Shall I paint one in?

speaker: Maitri
line: Many have. The trouble is that a guess painted in becomes the next person’s evidence. I will leave the clay as it is for now — but I understand the pull. A blank is uncomfortable.

speaker: Maitri
line: Then it stays. "We cannot read this" is a finding, and one of the most honest sentences in archaeology.

speaker: Maitri
line: Better still. Each reading claims something about the language behind the signs, and we can test those claims against the signs themselves. None has survived the test yet. Leave the line blank and we lose nothing.

speaker: Maitri
line: Hiranya has pressed a carnelian bead into your hand, etched, with a little boat on it. Beads like it turn up in Mesopotamia. That boat is going somewhere. Follow it across the water, to people who wrote everything down — and see what they say about us.

speaker: Bhadra
line: Ask me what the drains say and I can tell you. Ask me what the seals say, and I will tell you the truth: nobody knows. That is not the same as nothing.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Invaders massacred the people of Mohenjo-daro and ended the Indus civilisation.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The Indus cities were never planned. They just grew, like any other old town.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Lothal had the oldest dockyard in the world, and that is settled fact.

speaker: Maitri
line: Same centuries, same trade routes, opposite problem. These people wrote everything down. Tens of thousands of tablets, and still the Dhundh finds a way in.

speaker: Maitri
line: Notice how it feels to hold a source you can actually check. Keep that feeling. You will want it back later.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Writing settles everything. If it is not on a tablet, it did not happen. Those drains you admired? Unwritten. Forget them.

speaker: Maitri
line: You came to the writing end of the Gulf first. Remember this panel when you reach the Indus: this is what a readable record looks like.

speaker: Maitri
line: Ur-sin brings the goods in. But goods without a record are a rumour. Find the man who pays for them: Ea-nasir.

speaker: Maitri
line: Ea-nasir weighs it, prices it, and then it must be written down or it never happened. Take it to the Tablet House and find Nin-shubur.

speaker: Maitri
line: Sailor, merchant, scribe. Notice that the scribe is last — and is the only reason we know any of it. A famous complaint tablet to this very merchant has survived nearly four thousand years. Ordinary grievances last longer than kings do.

speaker: Nin-shubur
line: You read it! Years, that takes us. We start at seven. And what we practise is mostly lists: barley, beer, sheep. The poetry comes later.

speaker: Ea-nasir
line: Carnelian from Meluhha, copper from Magan, silver from the north. Weigh it right and nobody writes me a complaint. I have had one. Once.

speaker: Maitri
line: The second panel is back: a clay tablet in wedge-writing, and pressed beside it, the same sealed bead you carried from the Indus. Two panels, one thread between them. The first stitch.

speaker: Maitri
line: Someone has scratched a second line under the bead on the tablet: "The Indus traders were honest." Do we leave it there?

speaker: Maitri
line: It does sound nice. But who wrote it, and what did they know? A nice line with no source behind it is just a smudge with good manners. I will note it as a comment, not a record.

speaker: Maitri
line: Quite right. The first question about any line is who is speaking and what they could actually know. The tablets give us names, dates and prices. Honesty is a character reference. Show me the receipt.

speaker: Maitri
line: The last tablet in the pile is damp and chipped. A traveller’s note, copied from a trader, about a far land across the sea. It is not an account. It is a story. Different evidence, different rules. Time to learn the difference between a tablet and a tale.

speaker: Ea-nasir
where: Sumer & Dilmun · witness at the Sabha
line: You want to know whether a thing happened? Find the receipt. And then ask who wrote the receipt, and why.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Writing was invented to record poetry, prayers and the deeds of kings.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: There is no reason for sixty minutes in an hour. It is arbitrary, and nobody knows where it came from.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Mesopotamia and the Indus were one civilisation under two names.

speaker: Maitri
line: Different kind of evidence now. This is not a tablet and not a dig. It is a story, told for two thousand years by people who loved it. We are going to treat it exactly as that.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: There it is. One story. Why would you want three hundred of them?

speaker: Maitri
line: Because that is how it lived. Don’t answer it. It cannot hurt you if you do not answer.

speaker: Maitri
line: You started inside the epic. Fine — it is a good place to learn that a story can be true in a way a tablet cannot, and false in ways a tablet can.

speaker: Maitri
line: Revati grew up with a grandmother’s version. Fair enough. Now ask someone whose job is the forest: Guha, the boatman on the Sarayu.

speaker: Maitri
line: Guha’s version lingers on the river crossing, naturally. Two versions already, and neither one is wrong. One more: the young reciter, Lava.

speaker: Maitri
line: Three people, three tellings, one story. Nobody got it "wrong". Each told it from where they stood. That is how this kind of evidence behaves, and it is not a flaw. It is the thing you are reading.

speaker: Revati
line: My grandmother’s Ramayana was not my neighbour’s. Both of us were sure we had it right. We were both telling the truth about what the story was for.

speaker: Vaidya Sumitra
line: Some of what you picked is named in the text. Some of it has been identified by people with hand lenses and herbaria. Keep those two lists apart in your head.

speaker: Maitri
line: The third panel is back, and it is the strangest one yet: the same scene painted three times in three styles, side by side, none of them marked as the original.

speaker: Maitri
line: A child at the edge of the panel asks which of the three is the real one. What do I tell them?

speaker: Maitri
line: That is exactly what most of us do, and it is why the tradition has survived: we each keep the one we love. But it would be a small lie to call it the only one. I will tell them it is their favourite.

speaker: Maitri
line: That is the answer, and it is better than a ranking. Three tellings, three teachers, three reasons. They can love one and still read the other two.

speaker: Maitri
line: Guha rows you across the strait. At low tide the next shore has a causeway that does not quite break the surface. Is it a bridge, or a shoal? Ask the person who measured it, and then ask the person who tells the story. They are not the same person, and they do not need to be.

speaker: Revati
where: Kosala & Dandaka · witness at the Sabha
line: You are asking me whether it is true. I can tell you what it is for. If you want to know whether it is a dig report, you have already been to the dig.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The Ramayana is a news report. Every detail in it has been confirmed by archaeology.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: There is only one Ramayana. All the others are corruptions of it.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The story never left India. It is a local tale with no wider life.

speaker: Maitri
line: Low tide. Look down the line of the shoal. Two people on this shore are asking the same question, an age apart. Your job is to carry the answers between them.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The bridge is definitely man-made. Scientists agree. Why not simply say so? Everyone will be so pleased.

speaker: Maitri
line: Do they agree? Go and ask the person with the sounding line.

speaker: Maitri
line: You began at the water’s edge. It is a hard place to start — two kinds of truth meet here, and the Dhundh wants you to merge them.

speaker: Maitri
line: Nila reads the sounding line: shallow, then shallower, then a ridge. That is data. Now ask the geologist what the ridge is made of.

speaker: Maitri
line: Dr. Fernando says: old beach ridges, sand, coral. Natural. Now take that to the engineer, Nala, and see what the poem makes of the same sea.

speaker: Maitri
line: One shore, two questions, and no contradiction. The geologist says what the shoal is. The poet says what crossing it means. Neither is a worse kind of truth, only a different kind. Never ask one to do the other’s job.

speaker: Nala
where: The Setu & Lanka · after a challenge
line: We did not conjure it. We surveyed, we gathered, we organised teams. A causeway is a piece of logistics. The poet understood that, which is why the poem spends so long on it.

speaker: Trijata
where: The Setu & Lanka · after a challenge
line: Vibhishana crossed the water to the other side. Whatever you think of the reasons, that took more courage than anything the soldiers did. Ask yourself who fed them.

speaker: Maitri
where: The Setu & Lanka · restoring the panel
line: The fourth panel is back: a sea in the middle, and across it the Setu drawn as a faint dotted line — half bridge, half shoal, exactly as the evidence leaves it.

speaker: Maitri
where: The Setu & Lanka · restoring the panel
line: Someone asks me to firm up the dotted line into a solid one. "Just so it looks like a bridge." Shall I?

speaker: Maitri
where: The Setu & Lanka · restoring the panel
line: It would look better. People would remember it. And the next person who read the panel would think the surveyors had found a built bridge, which they have not. I will draw it as the evidence leaves it.

speaker: Maitri
where: The Setu & Lanka · restoring the panel
line: Dotted it stays. Notice how much that one line carries: the shoal that is there, the crossing the poem narrates, and the gap between them that we promised to keep honest.

speaker: Maitri
where: The Setu & Lanka · restoring the panel
line: Nala’s last word: "Every stone in that bridge was carried by someone. Remember that before the next battlefield." Beyond the strait the ground rises to a field where two armies stand facing each other.

speaker: Dr. Meena Fernando
where: The Setu & Lanka · witness at the Sabha
line: I will tell you what holds it up: sand, coral and a very old ridge. And I will tell you what the poet says holds it up: teams, planning and nerve. Neither of us is lying.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Adam’s Bridge is a man-made structure built thousands of years ago. Science has proved it.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The bridge in the Ramayana is just an invention. It tells us nothing worth knowing.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Ravana’s Lanka was a real city, found and mapped, exactly where the poem says.

speaker: Maitri
line: Dawn over the two camps. Eighteen days of war, and the longest poem in the world is really about a family that could not talk to itself. Read what Sanjaya actually says.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Good side, bad side. Eighteen days. Easy. Why would anyone want it complicated?

speaker: Maitri
line: Because it was complicated. You have heard that voice now at three borders. It does not get cleverer. It gets tidier.

speaker: Maitri
line: You came down on the field itself. Most people meet the Gita first. Notice that the poem takes eighteen days to get to the part everyone quotes, and then it spends a whole book on a conversation.

speaker: Maitri
line: Takshaka builds and mends the chariots. A chariot without a wright is a cart without a wheel. Now ask who fits the shafts of the arrows: the fletcher.

speaker: Maitri
line: Arrows, thousands of them, and every one made by a person. Take that to the healer who mends what the arrows do: Ashvini, the battlefield surgeon.

speaker: Maitri
line: A chariot, an arrow, a wound. Three people, and not one of them has a verse of their own. The epic is about the heroes. The war is about everyone behind them. The Dhundh would like you to forget that.

speaker: Sanjaya
line: I told the king what I saw and what I heard. I did not tell the king what to feel. That was the part the king could not forgive.

speaker: Shalya-putra
line: The bird’s eye. Fine. But I made the arrows, and nobody asked what I saw. Ask about Ekalavya, and what the teacher demanded. That is the other half of this lesson.

speaker: Maitri
line: The fifth panel is back: a wide field with two armies painted in the same colour. No side is marked as good. Beneath it, in thin script, a line in Sanjaya’s voice.

speaker: Maitri
line: The panel looks unsettled. I could tint one army gold and the other grey. It would be much easier to look at. Shall I?

speaker: Maitri
line: It is clearer. It is also not what the poem does. I will do it if you like — but I will remember that I did, and I will not be able to tell you the panel is faithful.

speaker: Maitri
line: The same colour, then. The poem knows what it is doing: the family that could not talk to itself loses the argument on both sides. Let the panel keep saying that.

speaker: Maitri
line: A good instinct, and Sanjaya would say the same: tell what you saw, do not tell people what to feel. I will not repaint a witness.

speaker: Maitri
line: Act II is done. You have handled the three hardest stories on this island without turning any of them into a lie. That is the whole method. Sanjaya hands you a rolled leaf: "Take this to the one who put regrets in stone." Now you meet the people who wrote things down on purpose.

speaker: Sanjaya
line: I will tell you what I saw and what I heard. I will not tell you what to feel about it. That was never my job.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The Mahabharata war happened in 3102 BCE. It is a fixed, proven date.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The epic is a simple story of heroes and villains. It never questions its own side.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The Gita is a transcript, taken down word for word on the battlefield.

speaker: Maitri
line: Finally an Indian voice we can read in the original, on the original stone. Ashoka’s edicts are the oldest Indian writing we can actually read. One of them is an apology.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: An emperor. Of course the emperor was perfect. Why spoil a good monument with details?

speaker: Maitri
line: The edict spoils it for you, and that is the point of the edict. Go and read it.

speaker: Maitri
line: You began where the writing starts to speak in its own voice. This is the panel that finishes the thought the Indus panel began: what it takes for a script to be read.

speaker: Maitri
line: Sunita cuts the stone. But stone does nothing until someone reads it. Find the one who walks the roads: Mahamatra Devi, the dhamma inspector.

speaker: Maitri
line: Devi inspects. Inspecting needs records, and records need clerks. Go and find the revenue officer, Amatya Rudradaman.

speaker: Maitri
line: Cutter, inspector, accountant. An order nobody can read is not an order — it is decoration, as the emperor himself says. All the work of an empire is the work of people in the middle. You have just walked through it.

speaker: Sunita
line: It took someone with a coin in one hand and a Greek legend in the other to read it again, many centuries later. We cut it. They read it back. I think we are even.

speaker: Mahamatra Devi
line: I walk the roads with the edict in my head. Wells, shade trees, rest-houses. Judge the dhamma by the wells, the emperor says. I have counted them. The emperor is not wrong.

speaker: Maitri
line: The sixth panel is back: a pillar with an inscription, and at its base a real line of Brahmi, the oldest Indian writing we can read. Look closely. Beside it, in very small letters, there is a scratch where someone has tried to add a word.

speaker: Maitri
line: The extra word is "mighty". I could leave it there. Many modern descriptions of this edict use it. Shall I?

speaker: Maitri
line: It fits a lot of things. But the edict is not a boast. It is the opposite: a public apology. I will keep the word as a comment on the panel, not on the stone.

speaker: Maitri
line: Scratched off. An emperor chose to have regret carved in public in the language of the subjects. No other ancient royal inscription does that. The panel should be as honest as the stone.

speaker: Maitri
line: A single line is picked out across the floor of the court, pointing south: "There is a country that kept its records on the walls of its temples. Every boundary, every tax, every ballot, carved in Tamil. Go and read it."

speaker: Sunita
line: The emperor’s name is on every pillar. Mine is on none. I am not complaining. I am pointing out which of us was holding the chisel.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Ashoka ordered every subject to become Buddhist.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The Kalinga casualty figures were invented by later chroniclers. Ashoka never confessed to anything.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Ashoka built the whole of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, gateways and all.

speaker: Maitri
line: A country that wrote its administration on the walls of its temples. Granite, bronze and village ballots drawn from a pot. This is the state measuring itself.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The Cholas had a democracy a thousand years ago. Say it. It is such a pleasing sentence.

speaker: Maitri
line: It is. Read the wall before you repeat it.

speaker: Maitri
line: You began among the temples. Good: this is the one place where the stone itself explains how the village chose its committees. Read the inscription before you read anyone’s summary of it.

speaker: Maitri
line: Ponni farms the delta. The harvest is taxed in rice. Now find the person who counts it: Karanattan, the temple accountant.

speaker: Maitri
line: Karanattan counts it, writes it and has it checked. Every figure on the wall is somebody’s signature on a promise. Go and ask the builder, Kunjaramallan, what the figures bought.

speaker: Maitri
line: Field, ledger, temple. The surprise of this chapter is how much of its glory is bookkeeping. The Cholas built tanks and temples because they could count what they had, and prove it on a wall. That is a better compliment than the word democracy.

speaker: Sembian
where: The Chola Country · after a challenge
line: Wax, clay, fire, metal, and break the mould. Every bronze is one of a kind because the mould dies to make it. Remember that next time someone calls a thing "mass produced".

speaker: Karanattan
where: The Chola Country · after a challenge
line: You saw the rule: anyone who had not submitted accounts was barred. Everyone who served had to be audited. That is the part I would carve in gold, if I were allowed.

speaker: Maitri
where: The Chola Country · restoring the panel
line: The seventh panel is back: granite and bronze, and a very small signature in the lower corner. Kunjaramallan’s. It is one of the smallest things on the whole island, and it is the one thing the panel could not do without.

speaker: Maitri
where: The Chola Country · restoring the panel
line: Someone suggests removing the signature so the temple looks like it was made by the god alone, with no human hand to distract. Shall I?

speaker: Maitri
where: The Chola Country · restoring the panel
line: It would look more serene. It would also be less true, and the builder signed it for a reason. I will cover it with a cloth for the pilgrims, and keep the signature underneath.

speaker: Maitri
where: The Chola Country · restoring the panel
line: Kept. The builder signed the stone, and then the temple stood for a thousand years. The signature outlived the argument about whether to put it there.

speaker: Maitri
where: The Chola Country · restoring the panel
line: Among the donations on the wall, a bronze Nataraja stands over a note about a sundial. Navigators and astronomers lived in the same century as these temple builders, and on the other coast a temple has been built as a chariot for the sun. Go and read the shadow.

speaker: Kunjaramallan
where: The Chola Country · witness at the Sabha
line: I signed it. It is small, and it is there. I wanted whoever came after to know that a person had done this, and that the person knew what they were doing.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The Chola village assemblies were a democracy, just like ours.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The tower of the great temple was lifted by a miracle. No engineering was involved.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The Cholas never left the coast. Medieval South India had no navy and no overseas reach.

speaker: Maitri
line: A temple built as a chariot, and instruments that tell the time by shadow. Look at those wheels. They are clocks.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Pretty carving. It does not mean anything. Take a photograph and move on.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Or: ancient India knew everything. Aircraft, atoms, all of it. Why check?

speaker: Maitri
line: You began with the wheels. The two voices you hear here are the same voice talking from opposite ends. Notice that they both tell you not to check.

speaker: Maitri
line: Divakara reads the wheel by its shadow. Fine — that is the stone. Ask the almanac-maker what the sky says: Panchangi Ratna.

speaker: Maitri
line: Panchangi Ratna compares the shadow with the almanac and finds them in agreement. Now find the instrument-maker who builds the dial: Kesari.

speaker: Maitri
line: A shadow, a table, a stone dial. Three ways of agreeing on what time it is, and all three have to match. That is what measurement means: an agreement that anyone can test. You can test this one with your hand.

speaker: Divakara
where: Konark & the Observatory · after a challenge
line: The spokes are exact. If they were uneven, the shadow would read a different hour on each side. A pretty thing that is wrong is not pretty to me. It is a broken clock.

speaker: Jagannatha Samrat
where: Konark & the Observatory · after a challenge
line: Aryabhata was contradicted, and rightly in places. That is how a tradition stays honest. Anyone who tells you Aryabhata was never wrong has not read the people who corrected the work.

speaker: Maitri
where: Konark & the Observatory · restoring the panel
line: The eighth panel is back: a great stone wheel, and in its rim a thin shadow-line that moves with the sun. It is the only panel on the island that is never quite the same twice.

speaker: Maitri
where: Konark & the Observatory · restoring the panel
line: A visitor asks whether I could freeze the shadow at noon. "Noon looks best in photographs." Shall I?

speaker: Maitri
where: Konark & the Observatory · restoring the panel
line: It is easier. But it turns a working instrument into a picture of one. I will make a copy for photographs and leave the real one moving.

speaker: Maitri
where: Konark & the Observatory · restoring the panel
line: Let it move. The wheel is only true while it is working, and the same is true of most of what we have been looking at.

speaker: Maitri
where: Konark & the Observatory · restoring the panel
line: Act III is done. Three chapters of people who wrote things down on purpose, and look how much even the scribes left out. Carved into the temple floor, a single line: "Ask who laid the stone."

speaker: Jagannatha Samrat
where: Konark & the Observatory · witness at the Sabha
line: We translated Euclid and the Almagest into Sanskrit, and we argued with all of it. A tradition that cannot be argued with is not a tradition. It is a monument.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Ancient Indian astronomers already knew everything modern science knows.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The wheels of the Sun Temple are decoration. They carry no information.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Zero is not an Indian idea. The numerals only came to Europe by accident.

speaker: Maitri
line: The most beautiful and the most dangerous place on the island. A city of granite boulders, canals still running, and one catastrophic afternoon. Be careful which of those three you let write the story.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: This city fell in an afternoon. What is the point of knowing it? It is gone. Let it be gone.

speaker: Maitri
line: You started in the ruin. Of all places to begin — it is the one with an afternoon in it. Walk gently, and remember the water is still running.

speaker: Maitri
line: Allasani Peddana sings the court — and a court poet does not sing about the canal-keeper. Remember what is missing. Now ask the foreigner: the envoy from Herat, Abdur Razzaq.

speaker: Maitri
line: An envoy sees the city as a stranger does, and writes for a ruler at home. Two witnesses, two different silences. Last: the horse-trader, Nuniz.

speaker: Maitri
line: A poet, an envoy and a trader. Each tells the truth, each for a different reader, and none of them mentions the canal-keeper. A source is not just what it says. It is also what its author had no reason to say.

speaker: Hampamma
line: The canals were never abandoned. We have been keeping the water since before the city fell. Ask the people who write about the fall how many of them have walked a canal at dawn.

speaker: Nuniz
line: I wrote down what I saw, which was a rich city at the height of a king’s power, and I wrote it for people who wanted horses sold. Keep that in mind when you read me.

speaker: Maitri
line: The ninth panel is back, and it is half-painted on purpose: the city before, and the ruin after, with a single stitched line of canal running through both.

speaker: Maitri
line: I could paint over the join, so the city and the ruin look like one continuous picture. It would be easier on the eye. Shall I?

speaker: Maitri
line: They do. That is why the afternoon story lasted. But it would hide the one line that runs through both halves, and that line is the most important thing on the panel. I will leave a hairline.

speaker: Maitri
line: Left as it is. The canal runs through the join because it kept running. That is what the evidence says, and the evidence is better than the afternoon.

speaker: Maitri
line: I will tell you something, and then I will go quiet for a while. You can mend a ruin on a panel. You cannot mend a ruin. Bichitr’s miniature in the next court shows a white dome, a garden and a great many people. Go and ask who built it.

speaker: Mallappa
line: I cut stone. Ask me about the afternoon and I will tell you what I saw, which was people carrying water in the evening, same as always.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The Stone Chariot at Hampi is carved from a single block of granite.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Vijayanagara was wiped out in a single afternoon in 1565, and nothing of it survived.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: The water canals of Vijayanagara are a legend. Nothing like them has been found.

speaker: Maitri
line: Marble geometry, a garden laid out as paradise, and an emperor who held debates. This is where the Gilder does its best work.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: A monument to love. Nobody was harmed. The builders were happy. Look at it! Who would ruin that?

speaker: Maitri
line: The people who are not in the picture would, if they were asked. Let’s ask.

speaker: Maitri
line: You started at the Taj. It is the hardest place to look past, which is why it is the best place to practise. Look at the white, and then look at the edges.

speaker: Maitri
line: Puran brings marble from Makrana and cuts it to size. Nobody put a name on it. Now find the apprentice who cuts the inlay: Zarina.

speaker: Maitri
line: Zarina cuts the petals to a hair. The border will carry that work for four hundred years, and the name of its cutter nowhere. Last: Bhishti Ramzan, who carries the water that mortars every wall.

speaker: Maitri
line: Quarry, inlay, water. Nobody on this trail signed the building, and every one of them is in the record of what it took. The marble is one thing. The twenty thousand are another. The Taj is both.

speaker: Zarina
line: Every petal is cut to a hair. If it is off by a grain of sand, the whole border shows it. We learn it by doing it wrong for a year.

speaker: Bichitr
line: I painted what I was shown. The court asked me to paint it kind. Ask yourself who commissions a picture, and who does not.

speaker: Maitri
line: The tenth panel is back: the Taj in white, and a section of the border left deliberately unpainted. A tiny label beneath it reads: "for Puran, and the others".

speaker: Maitri
line: A visitor offers to fill the blank with an invented name, a beautiful one, so the border looks finished. "It would be a kindness." Shall I?

speaker: Maitri
line: It would feel like one. But a name we invented is not a name the person had, and the next visitor would read it as a record. A lovely lie is still a lie. I will keep it as a story, not a signature.

speaker: Maitri
line: Blank, then, and labelled. Someone made this border, and we do not know who. Saying so is the only respect we can offer that is also true.

speaker: Maitri
line: Bichitr’s miniature, in the last gallery of the atelier, shows a fort on a hill in the west, a man on a horse, and a cistern cut into the rock. It is not an emperor’s picture. Go and see it.

where: Agra & Sikri · witness at the Sabha

line: The last chapter. Forts, queens, spies, water, and a lot of historians arguing. Where geography is the general. Notice how many of the great stories here are really about hydrology.

speaker: Ekarupa

speaker: Ekarupa

speaker: Maitri
line: Balaji keeps the ledger. A ledger is not a chronicle; it records what was spent, not what was felt. Now go and ask the armourer who the money was spent on: Sakharam.

speaker: Maitri
line: Sakharam’s work is on the ledger and nowhere else. Last stop: the hill scout, Yesaji, who knows what the ledger does not.

speaker: Maitri
line: A clerk, a smith, a scout. The ledger tells you what was spent. The scout tells you what it was spent on. Neither is the chronicle, and each corrects the other. Almost all history is that: someone checking one record against another.

speaker: Ahilyabai Holkar
where: The Hill Forts · after a challenge

speaker: Tanaji
where: The Hill Forts · after a challenge

speaker: Maitri
where: The Hill Forts · restoring the panel

speaker: Maitri
where: The Hill Forts · restoring the panel
line: The clerk offers to "tidy up" a discrepancy in the ledger, one small figure that does not match, so the fort’s account reads more heroically. Shall I let the clerk?

speaker: Maitri
where: The Hill Forts · restoring the panel
line: It would read better. It would also be the exact thing the Dhundh does, in the smallest possible way: one figure, nudged to flatter. I will keep the original in a note, so the nudge can be found.

speaker: Maitri
where: The Hill Forts · restoring the panel
line: Left. A figure that does not match is a clue: a repair, a loan, a mistake, a lie. Tidied, it would tell us nothing. Untidied, it still might.

speaker: Maitri
where: The Hill Forts · restoring the panel
line: That is the eleventh panel. All of them are hanging in the air around you, and they do not quite touch. Three threads run across all of them, in the wrong order, tangled. Now we find out what you have learned. Open the scroll and call the Sabha.

speaker: Sakhubai
where: The Hill Forts · witness at the Sabha
line: You want to know why the fort held? Ask what was in the tank. Everything else is a story we tell about the tank.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Haldighati was a clear and total victory for one side.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Hill forts were held by courage alone. Water and stone had little to do with it.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Ahilyabai Holkar was only a figurehead. The real work was done by the men around the throne, and almost nothing of Ahilyabai’s own survives.

speaker: Kaushi
line: Tide’s turning. If the boat is not loaded before the water drops, it waits a day.

speaker: Kaushi
line: Carnelian out, copper and silver in. Keep the weights honest and the Gulf keeps buying.

speaker: Kaushi
line: That basin is lined with burnt brick, two hundred metres of it. Someone planned this before a single boat came.

speaker: Ashvini
line: A long carnelian bead takes days. Heat the stone, flake it, grind it, then drill — and the drill is harder than the stone.

speaker: Ashvini
line: They want our beads in Ur. I have never seen Ur. My beads have.

speaker: Ashvini
line: The trick is the drill bit: a stone we call ernestite, cooked until it bites.

speaker: Hiranya
line: One brick, two brick, four brick. Length twice the width, width twice the height. Always.

speaker: Hiranya
line: Lay the main streets north-south first. Everything else follows the grid.

speaker: Hiranya
line: A city without drains is a village with ambitions.

speaker: Bhadra
line: Lift the slab, clear the silt, set the slab back. Every lane, every month.

speaker: Bhadra
line: You can tell a careless household by its soak-pit. I know who they are.

speaker: Bhadra
line: The city pays me. Think about what that means — somebody decided this job was worth wages.

speaker: Sujata
line: Cotton. We were spinning it here before anyone else anywhere, whatever the Egyptians say about linen.

speaker: Sujata
line: Dyed with madder for red. The colour holds if the mordant is right.

speaker: Sujata
line: They ship my cloth west in bales. Nobody there will know my name.

speaker: Nilu
role: A child of the lower town
line: Look — a clay bull with a nodding head. My uncle made it. Pull the string.

speaker: Nilu
role: A child of the lower town
line: There are little carts too, with real wheels that turn. And whistles shaped like birds.

speaker: Nilu
role: A child of the lower town
line: Grown-ups think the seals are the important things. The toys are better.

speaker: Hemaka
line: Wheat and barley in the cool season. Sesame and cotton after. The river decides, not me.

speaker: Hemaka
line: We sow into the mud the flood leaves behind. No flood, no sowing.

speaker: Hemaka
line: My field is ploughed in two directions, crossways. Try it — the yield is better.

speaker: Dr. Ila Rao
where: Sindhu-Sarasvati · Why Did the Cities Empty?
line: You are standing on nine metres of other people’s rubbish, and I mean that as a compliment. Every layer is a century. Around 1900 BCE the top layers change: the big public buildings stop being maintained, the weights stop being standard, the long-distance trade goods thin out. People do not vanish — they move, and they live differently. The question is why.

speaker: Dr. Ila Rao
where: Sindhu-Sarasvati · Why Did the Cities Empty?
line: That was the old story — Mortimer Wheeler once read a group of skeletons at Mohenjo-daro as a massacre. Later study showed those skeletons are from different periods and mostly show no battle wounds. There is no destruction layer, no burnt citadel, no mass of foreign weapons. Migration into the subcontinent in the second millennium BCE is well supported by linguistics and ancient DNA, but it is not the same claim as a war that ended the cities.

speaker: Dr. Ila Rao
where: Sindhu-Sarasvati · Why Did the Cities Empty?
line: Over-read. The bones did not say what the headline said.

speaker: Dr. Ila Rao
where: Sindhu-Sarasvati · Why Did the Cities Empty?
line: Water. Palaeoclimate records — lake sediments, stalagmites, ocean cores — show the summer monsoon weakening after about 2200 BCE across a wide belt from Mesopotamia to the Indus. At the same time the Ghaggar-Hakra system in the east was drying and the Indus itself was shifting channels. Cities that depended on predictable floodwater farming and on river transport lose both at once.

speaker: Dr. Ila Rao
where: Sindhu-Sarasvati · Why Did the Cities Empty?
line: Settlement counts tell the story: sites in the west and on the Hakra decline, while sites in Haryana, Punjab and Gujarat increase. The population shifted east and south into smaller villages. Pottery traditions continue. Farming continues. What ends is the *city system* — the standard weights, the seals, the great public works. Civilisations rarely die. They reorganise.

speaker: Nin-shubur
line: I have copied the sign for barley nine hundred times. My teacher says nine hundred more.

speaker: Nin-shubur
line: Clay is patient. Dry it, and the receipt outlives the merchant, the king and the city.

speaker: Nin-shubur
line: They bring seals from Meluhha. Pretty animals. Nobody here can read the signs either.

speaker: Ea-nasir
line: Copper from Magan, beads from Meluhha, silver from the north. I take my cut from all three.

speaker: Ea-nasir
line: A customer once wrote me a tablet of complaints about my copper. People still talk about it.

speaker: Ea-nasir
line: Sixty shekels to the mina. Learn it or be cheated.

speaker: Ninkasi-udug
line: Barley bread, soaked and fermented, strained through a mat. Everyone is paid partly in beer.

speaker: Ninkasi-udug
line: The ration tablets list it by the jar. That is most of what writing is for here.

speaker: Ninkasi-udug
line: There is a hymn to the goddess of brewing that doubles as the recipe. Clever, that.

speaker: Ur-sin
line: Hug the coast, anchor at night, never lose sight of land if you can help it.

speaker: Ur-sin
line: Dilmun first, then Magan. Only fools run straight for Meluhha.

speaker: Ur-sin
line: Reed boats caulked with bitumen. The bitumen seeps out of the ground here — the gods were generous.

speaker: Nabu-rimanni
line: Every night, on a tablet: the moon’s place, the planets, the weather, the price of barley.

speaker: Nabu-rimanni
line: Centuries of these. That is how we learned the eclipses come round in a cycle.

speaker: Nabu-rimanni
line: Observe, record, wait. Most of astronomy is patience written down.

speaker: Enheduanna-sal
line: Houses, boats, baskets, pens, writing styluses. All of it reed.

speaker: Enheduanna-sal
line: We bend the bundles into arches and tie them. No nails, no timber — there are no trees here.

speaker: Enheduanna-sal
line: The marsh feeds us when the canals fail. The city forgets that until it happens.

speaker: Revati
line: Fourteen years the city kept its lamps lit, they say. My grandmother’s grandmother made those lamps.

speaker: Revati
line: A city is not its palace. A city is its potters, its weavers and its drains.

speaker: Revati
line: Diwali? We have lit lamps for the returning for as long as anyone remembers.

speaker: Guha
line: I ferried a prince across this river once. He paid me nothing and I asked for nothing.

speaker: Guha
line: The forest is not empty. It is full of people the city forgets to count.

speaker: Guha
line: Follow the birds to water. They know the fords better than the maps.

speaker: Lava
line: We learned it by ear, in metre, thousands of verses. The metre is what holds it in the memory.

speaker: Lava
line: Our teacher says we are singing a man his own story and he has not recognised it yet.

speaker: Lava
line: Anustubh: eight syllables, four times over. Once you have the rhythm the words follow it.

speaker: Vaidya Sumitra
line: First identify. Then the season, then the part — root, bark, leaf, fruit. Each has its hour.

speaker: Vaidya Sumitra
line: Half of what I do is setting bones and cleaning wounds. The herbs get the stories.

speaker: Vaidya Sumitra
line: Learn three plants properly rather than thirty by rumour.

speaker: Sthapati Jiva
line: Everything you admire in stone later was first worked out in timber. The brackets, the eaves, the railings.

speaker: Sthapati Jiva
line: Sal for beams, teak where we can get it. Season it two years or it will twist on you.

speaker: Sthapati Jiva
line: Stone copies wood for centuries before it learns to be stone.

speaker: Ira
line: Wheel-thrown, not coiled. You can see the throwing rings inside if you look.

speaker: Ira
line: Archaeologists will date us by our rubbish, my teacher says. So throw it away neatly.

speaker: Ira
line: Every village makes a slightly different rim. That is how you tell where a pot has been.

speaker: Kavi Sumant
line: You want the true Ramayana? Careful what you ask a bard. I have sung it in Awadhi for farmers, heard it chanted in Tamil at a temple, and watched it danced in masks on an island where nobody speaks a word of Sanskrit. Which of those was false?

speaker: Kavi Sumant
line: It is the oldest we have, yes — seven kandas, some twenty-four thousand verses, composed and reshaped over centuries. But "oldest surviving" is not the same as "the one everyone means". When a child in Varanasi says Ramayana she usually means Tulsidas’s Ramcharitmanas, written in Awadhi in the sixteenth century, and she is not making a mistake.

speaker: Kavi Sumant
line: Now you are listening like a scholar.

speaker: Kavi Sumant
line: Kamban’s Ramavataram in Tamil, around the twelfth century. Molla’s Telugu Ramayanam, by a potter’s daughter. Krittibas in Bengali. Ezhuthachan in Malayalam. Madhava Kandali in Assamese. Sant Eknath in Marathi. The Jain Paumacariya, which makes Ravana a tragic, dignified figure. Each poet chose what to expand and what to leave out.

speaker: Kavi Sumant
line: Thailand sings the Ramakien and paints it along the walls of the royal temple in Bangkok. Java has the Kakawin Ramayana in Old Javanese and a shadow-puppet tradition that runs all night. Cambodia has the Reamker, Laos the Phra Lak Phra Lam, Malaysia the Hikayat Seri Rama, Myanmar the Yama Zatdaw. The story crossed the Bay of Bengal with traders and monks, long before passports.

speaker: Kavi Sumant
line: It does. And every place made it their own.

speaker: Kavi Sumant
line: Sharply. In some tellings Ravana is a learned king brought down by one fatal flaw; in the Jain version he is almost noble. Some retellings centre Sita’s suffering and judge Rama for it. Some end at the return to Ayodhya and refuse to tell the Uttara Kanda at all. The scholar A. K. Ramanujan wrote a famous essay about this and called them many Ramayanas. The right question is never "which is true", but "what is this particular telling trying to say?"

speaker: Nala
line: Do not ask me for the biggest stone. Ask me for the shallowest line.

speaker: Nala
line: Stone sinks. Stone on stone on a shoal does not. The sea does half the work if you let it.

speaker: Nala
line: They will sing about the army. They should sing about the sounding line.

speaker: Dr. Meena Fernando
line: The shoal chain is real and you can walk much of it at low tide. Coral, sand, and old beach ridges.

speaker: Dr. Meena Fernando
line: Sea-level cores put these banks in the hundreds of thousands of years. That is older than any story.

speaker: Dr. Meena Fernando
line: Two true things: the shoal is natural, and the epic is meaningful. Neither needs the other to be false.

speaker: Mannar
line: These banks have given pearls since before anyone kept records. Rome bought them. Everyone bought them.

speaker: Mannar
line: Down on one breath, stone in hand to sink faster, basket round the neck.

speaker: Mannar
line: Three minutes if the sea is kind. It is usually not.

speaker: Angada
line: Fires on the headlands. One for sighted, two for coming in, three for turn back.

speaker: Angada
line: Faster than any runner. The whole coast knows within the hour.

speaker: Angada
line: They will say the message flew. In a way it did.

speaker: Trijata
line: An army crosses on rice, not on courage. Count the sacks before you count the spears.

speaker: Trijata
line: Salt fish and tamarind keep. Everything else spoils in three days in this heat.

speaker: Trijata
line: Nobody writes poems about the quartermaster.

speaker: Nila
line: Knotted rope, lead weight, and you call the depth out loud so the boat behind hears it.

speaker: Nila
line: Find the shallow line and the sea builds half your road for you.

speaker: Nila
line: Measure twice at slack tide. Measuring on the ebb will lie to you.

speaker: Vibhishana
role: Brother to the king of Lanka
line: My brother has taken another man’s wife by force and will not return her. I have said so in open court. He called me a traitor and told me to leave. Stranger, I have one night to decide. Do I stand with my blood, or against it?

speaker: Vibhishana
role: Brother to the king of Lanka
line: Then I would be a man who knew better and stayed silent. The epic has a word for the advisor who flatters a king into ruin, and it is not a kind word. Kumbhakarna, my other brother, chooses exactly this: he tells Ravana plainly that he is wrong, and then fights for him anyway, and dies. He is not a villain. He is a warning.

speaker: Vibhishana
role: Brother to the king of Lanka
line: And honesty without courage is just noise.

speaker: Vibhishana
role: Brother to the king of Lanka
line: I have. Three times. In court, in his chamber, and on the terrace at dawn. He does not lack information. He lacks the willingness to be wrong in front of people. That is a different illness, and no argument cures it. At some point counsel ends and choice begins.

speaker: Vibhishana
role: Brother to the king of Lanka
line: Then I go, and I will be called a traitor in my own city for as long as the story is told. And in some tellings I am. But consider what the epic does with me afterwards: Rama makes me king of Lanka. Not as a reward for switching sides — as a statement about what a kingdom owes its people. Dharma, in this poem, is not whose side you are on. It is what you are willing to lose to do right.

speaker: Sanjaya
line: I describe this field to a king who cannot see it. He asks for details and then asks me to stop.

speaker: Sanjaya
line: The whole poem reaches you through someone retelling it. Remember that.

speaker: Sanjaya
line: Dhritarashtra’s first question is not who won. It is what my sons did.

speaker: Takshaka
line: Spoked wheel, bent-wood rim, two horses or four. A chariot is a workshop that someone decided to fight from.

speaker: Takshaka
line: They praise the archer. Nobody praises the axle, and the axle decides the battle.

speaker: Takshaka
line: Karna’s wheel sank in soft ground. That is not fate. That is drainage.

speaker: Shalya-putra
line: Three feathers, set with a slight spiral so the shaft spins. A straight-fletched arrow wanders.

speaker: Shalya-putra
line: Reed shafts for volume, bamboo for the good ones. Iron heads, barbed or bodkin.

speaker: Shalya-putra
line: I have made forty thousand arrows this month. Somebody will claim they shot them all.

speaker: Ashvini
line: Arrow out, wound cleaned, honey and ghee on it, bind it. Honey keeps a wound sweet.

speaker: Ashvini
line: The texts give a hundred and twenty-one instruments. I carry nine and improvise.

speaker: Ashvini
line: They bring me boys. Every single day, boys.

speaker: Sumantra
line: Conch at dawn to begin, conch at sunset to stop. Those were the terms both sides agreed.

speaker: Sumantra
line: I have blown the sunset conch and watched men keep fighting. That is the day it changed.

speaker: Sumantra
line: My voice carries further than an arrow. It is the only weapon I am allowed.

speaker: Uttara
line: There is a whole book about us, at the end. The women walking the field afterwards.

speaker: Uttara
line: They name the heroes. The poem at least has the decency to name the grief too.

speaker: Uttara
line: Ask who won and then ask who is left. They are different questions.

speaker: The Charioteer
where: Kurukshetra · The Conversation Between the Armies
line: Look at him. The finest archer of the age, sitting down in his own chariot with his bow on the floor. He says: these are my teachers and my cousins, and I would rather be killed than win this. The whole poem — seven hundred verses, eighteen chapters — begins from that collapse. What would you say to him?

speaker: The Charioteer
where: Kurukshetra · The Conversation Between the Armies
line: That is the crude reading, and it is the one people reach for when they have only heard of the text. The Gita never says "a promise is a promise, go kill". It spends its first chapters taking Arjuna’s grief seriously. An argument that does not take the objection seriously is not an argument; it is an order.

speaker: The Charioteer
where: Kurukshetra · The Conversation Between the Armies
line: Hold that thought, because the poem does consider it. Arjuna proposes exactly this and Krishna calls it what it is: not renunciation but paralysis dressed as virtue. Here is the trap — Arjuna is not choosing between acting and not acting. Standing still at Kurukshetra is itself an act with consequences for everyone behind him. There is no neutral square on this board.

speaker: The Charioteer
where: Kurukshetra · The Conversation Between the Armies
line: That is the hinge of the whole argument.

speaker: The Charioteer
where: Kurukshetra · The Conversation Between the Armies
line: Sometimes, yes — and the text respects genuine renunciation deeply. But it distinguishes it from flinching. True renunciation gives up the *fruit* of the action, not the action. The sannyasi who walks into the forest and the warrior who does his work without craving the prize are doing the same inner thing. Arjuna is not doing either yet; he is frozen.

speaker: The Charioteer
where: Kurukshetra · The Conversation Between the Armies
line: Then listen to what he actually says. His mouth is dry, his skin burns, his bow slips, he cannot stand. He is not reasoning — he is in shock, and the shock is about outcome: who will die, what will be destroyed, what people will say of him. Krishna’s answer goes straight at that. Do the work that is yours to do. Release your grip on the result. "Yoga-sthah kuru karmani" — established in steadiness, perform your actions.

speaker: The Charioteer
where: Kurukshetra · The Conversation Between the Armies
line: No — and this is where most summaries go wrong. You still choose the right action, carefully, by your duty and your conscience. What you let go of is the craving and the dread that distort the choosing. The surgeon who wants to be praised operates worse than the surgeon who wants the patient to live. That is nishkama karma: action without the hunger for its fruit.

speaker: The Charioteer
where: Kurukshetra · The Conversation Between the Armies
line: Exactly. Equanimity sharpens judgement; it does not switch it off.

speaker: The Charioteer
where: Kurukshetra · The Conversation Between the Armies
line: Then you have the Mahabharata’s other hundred thousand verses, which are largely about exactly that. The epic is full of people who obey badly chosen duties and are ruined — Bhishma’s vow, Karna’s loyalty, Dhritarashtra’s silence. The poem does not hand you a rule. It hands you the hardest cases and refuses to make them easy.

speaker: The Charioteer
where: Kurukshetra · The Conversation Between the Armies
line: And it offers more than one road. Karma yoga, the discipline of action. Jnana yoga, the discipline of knowledge. Bhakti yoga, the discipline of devotion. Dhyana, the discipline of meditation. The text does not insist that everyone is a warrior. It insists that everyone has work, and that how you hold your work matters as much as what the work is.

speaker: Sunita
line: Chunar sandstone. One block, thirteen metres, no joints. Getting it here was the hard part.

speaker: Sunita
line: The polish is the signature. Run your hand across it — two thousand years and still like glass.

speaker: Sunita
line: The lion capital from Sarnath is on your money now, I am told. We only carved it.

speaker: Bhikkhu Dharmapala
line: Students come from Tibet, China, Korea, Java, Sri Lanka. The entrance debate turns most of them away.

speaker: Bhikkhu Dharmapala

speaker: Bhikkhu Dharmapala
line: Nine storeys of manuscripts in the Dharmaganja. Copying is a form of prayer here.

speaker: Amatya Rudradaman
line: One-sixth of the harvest, by the book. Kautilya has a chapter on what to do when it is not paid.

speaker: Amatya Rudradaman
line: The Arthashastra is not a book about ethics. It is a book about what works, which is why it is uncomfortable.

speaker: Amatya Rudradaman
line: Spies, granaries, roads, irrigation. An empire is logistics wearing a crown.

line: I inspect: are the wells dug, the trees planted, the rest-houses standing, the prisoners treated properly.

speaker: Mahamatra Devi
line: The edicts are instructions to me as much as announcements to you.

speaker: Mahamatra Devi
line: A policy with no inspector is a wish.

speaker: Jnanashri
line: We copy texts to take home. A manuscript is worth more than a horse on that road.

speaker: Lohita
line: Magadha has iron and forests to burn into charcoal. That is the whole secret of this empire.

speaker: Lohita

speaker: Lohita
line: There is a pillar at Delhi that has not rusted in centuries. Someone here worked out why.

line: We carry a cutting of the bodhi tree to Lanka. A sapling travels better than an argument.

speaker: Bhikkhuni Sanghamitta
line: Donate a railing post and your name is cut into it. Look — half of them are women’s names.
