line: I have taken Kalinga. The scribes give me a number: a hundred and fifty thousand deported, a hundred thousand killed, many times that number dead afterwards of hunger and sickness. I have never been given numbers after a victory before. I asked for them. Now my stonecutters wait, and I do not know what to tell them to write.

speaker: Devanampiya Piyadasi
line: Every king before me has done exactly that. Mine would be one more boast in one more language on one more rock, and the kings who read it would copy it. But I have begun to think that a king who can only be obeyed out of fear has to keep producing fear, and the supply is finite.

speaker: Devanampiya Piyadasi
line: Forgetting is a luxury of the people who were not there. And I find I cannot. The edict I am considering contains a sentence no royal inscription has contained before: that the emperor feels remorse. My advisors think it is weakness. I think it is the only durable thing I own.

speaker: Devanampiya Piyadasi
line: Then that is what the rock will say. And I will go further. The edicts will not be in the court’s Sanskrit but in the Prakrit people actually speak, in Brahmi where it is read and in Kharosthi in the north-west, and in Greek and Aramaic where my subjects read those. An order nobody can read is not an order. It is decoration.

speaker: Devanampiya Piyadasi
line: No. Read Rock Edict 12 when it is cut. It says that one should not praise one’s own sect and disparage another’s, that whoever does so from devotion damages the very thing they are devoted to. I pay for Buddhist, Brahmanical, Jain and Ajivika establishments alike. I am a Buddhist layman; my edicts are not a conversion order.

speaker: Devanampiya Piyadasi
line: Concretely: obedience to parents and elders, decent treatment of servants and the poor, generosity to ascetics of every sect, restraint in speech, and non-injury to living beings. I have planted shade trees and dug wells along the roads, set up rest-houses, appointed dhamma-mahamatras to inspect. I have given up the royal hunt. Judge me by the wells, not by the verbs.

speaker: Kunjaramallan
line: No mortar. Not one measure of it in the tower. The stones are cut to hold each other.

speaker: Kunjaramallan
line: The shadow of the vimana does not fall on the ground at noon. Work out why.

speaker: Kunjaramallan
line: Every wage, every grant, every dancer’s name — carved on the wall. A temple is also an account book.

speaker: Sembian
line: Every mould is broken to free the figure. That is why no two of our bronzes are the same.

speaker: Sembian
line: Five metals, they say — pancha loha. Mostly copper, with tin, and a little of the others.

speaker: Sembian
line: The Nataraja has to balance on one foot and still be processional. Weight distribution is theology here.

speaker: Nangai
line: Four hundred of us are listed on that wall, with our names, our streets and our allowances.

speaker: Nangai
line: The poses in the stone are the poses we hold. The sculptors watched us; we check ourselves against them.

speaker: Nangai
line: Being written into a wall is not the same as being free. Both things are true.

speaker: Karanattan
line: Paddy in, oil in, wages out, lamps lit. Every figure goes on the wall where anyone can check it.

speaker: Karanattan
line: We measure land in veli and ma, and we survey it again when the river moves.

speaker: Karanattan
line: The stone does not forget and it cannot be edited. That is the point of it.

speaker: Kadal Arasan
line: Planks stitched with coir, not nailed. A sewn hull gives in a swell instead of splitting.

speaker: Kadal Arasan
line: Teak from the hills, coir from the coast, resin for the seams. All of it within a week’s cart ride.

speaker: Kadal Arasan
line: Repairs on a beach with no forge. Try that with an iron-nailed ship.

speaker: Ponni
line: Transplanted by hand, every seedling. Three crops a year where the water reaches.

speaker: Ponni
line: The tank committee fines you if you let your bund break. Quite right too.

speaker: Ponni
line: Kaveri water is counted out in days, not litres. Your turn comes round and you take it.

speaker: Nachchiyar
where: The Chola Country · The Pot Ballot
line: Before we draw, the rules are read aloud. They are not in a book that can be edited — they are cut into that wall, where everyone can check them. Sabha business, Uttaramerur, in the reign of Parantaka. Shall I read the qualifications or the disqualifications first?

speaker: Nachchiyar
where: The Chola Country · The Pot Ballot
line: A candidate must own a certain extent of tax-paying land, live in a house on his own site, be between roughly thirty-five and seventy years of age, and know the Vedas or at least the prescribed texts. Note what that means: there is a property qualification and a literacy qualification. This is not universal suffrage. It is a rule-bound, written, auditable local government — which in the tenth century is remarkable enough.

speaker: Nachchiyar
where: The Chola Country · The Pot Ballot
line: Barred: anyone who has not submitted his accounts; anyone whose relatives have not submitted theirs; anyone who took the committee seat in the last three years; anyone convicted of certain offences; anyone who rode the village’s business for private gain. Audit first, then eligibility. The inscription is blunt about it.

speaker: Nachchiyar
where: The Chola Country · The Pot Ballot
line: That is the sentence I would carve.

speaker: Nachchiyar
where: The Chola Country · The Pot Ballot
line: Each ward writes its eligible names on palm-leaf tickets. All tickets go into a pot — a kudam. A young boy who cannot read, so he cannot favour anyone, draws one ticket per ward in full view of the assembly. We call it kudavolai, the pot-ticket. Terms do not repeat for three years. Then the accounts are read again next year, and the wall does not forget.

speaker: Bisu Maharana
line: Twenty-four wheels, seven horses. The whole temple is the sun’s chariot, and it is meant to be read as one.

speaker: Bisu Maharana
line: Put your finger at the hub and watch the shadow cross the spokes. That is the time.

speaker: Bisu Maharana
line: The great tower fell. The porch stands. Sand and salt are patient enemies.

speaker: Jagannatha Samrat
line: His Highness had Euclid translated, and Ptolemy, and the tables from Samarkand. Then he built in stone.

speaker: Jagannatha Samrat
line: Why so large? Because a shadow on a 27-metre gnomon can be read to seconds. Small instruments lie politely.

speaker: Jagannatha Samrat
line: We compared our tables with the European ones and published where we differed. That is the job.

speaker: Divakara
line: Put your finger on the axle and read where the shadow crosses. That is the hour, to the quarter.

speaker: Divakara
line: Cloudy days we use a water clock — a bowl with a hole, sinking at a known rate.

speaker: Divakara
line: The temple is a chariot and a clock at the same time. Nobody thought that was odd.

speaker: Panchangi Ratna
line: Lunar months, solar year, and an extra month every three years to stop them drifting apart.

speaker: Panchangi Ratna
line: Farmers want the monsoon date. Priests want the festival date. I compute both from the same tables.

speaker: Panchangi Ratna
line: When my prediction is wrong the whole village knows by evening.

speaker: Kesari
line: An error of one finger-width on a scale this long is an error of seconds in the reading.

speaker: Kesari
line: We set the gnomon to the latitude. Get that wrong and nothing else can be right.

speaker: Kesari
line: Stone moves with the heat. We cut the scales at dawn.

speaker: Sumitra
line: We navigate by the temple. Painted black with sea salt — the sailors called it the Black Pagoda.

speaker: Sumitra
line: When it fell, boats went aground for a season until we learned new marks.

speaker: Sumitra
line: A monument is a landmark before it is a monument.

speaker: Aryabhata
where: Konark & the Observatory · The Earth Does Not Stand Still
line: I am twenty-three and I have finished the book. One hundred and twenty-one verses, four chapters, and in it I say something my teachers will not enjoy: that the stars do not go round us. We turn. Just as a man in a moving boat sees the bank slide backwards, so a man on a turning Earth sees the fixed stars slide west.

speaker: Aryabhata
where: Konark & the Observatory · The Earth Does Not Stand Still
line: Everyone can see the bank move, too. Appearance is the thing to be explained, not the explanation. And note what my model buys: one Earth turning once accounts for the daily motion of every star at once, instead of each sphere being pushed separately. The simpler account that predicts the same sky is the better account.

speaker: Aryabhata
where: Konark & the Observatory · The Earth Does Not Stand Still
line: By prediction. I give the length of the sidereal day as 23 hours, 56 minutes and about 4.1 seconds. Check it against the stars for a year; if I am wrong, the error accumulates and you will catch me. That is the whole discipline: commit to a number, then let the sky audit you. Later astronomers — Brahmagupta among them — attacked parts of my system hard, and some of their corrections were right.

speaker: Aryabhata
where: Konark & the Observatory · The Earth Does Not Stand Still
line: I would rather be corrected than consulted.

speaker: Aryabhata
where: Konark & the Observatory · The Earth Does Not Stand Still
line: The moon has no light of its own; it shines by the sun. A lunar eclipse is the Earth’s shadow falling across it; a solar eclipse is the moon’s shadow falling on us. No demon, no serpent swallowing anything. And because it is geometry, it can be computed in advance — I give methods for the size and duration of the shadow.

speaker: Aryabhata
where: Konark & the Observatory · The Earth Does Not Stand Still
line: Add four to one hundred, multiply by eight, add sixty-two thousand: for a diameter of twenty thousand, the circumference is 62,832. That is 3.1416. And I attach one word to it — asanna, approximate. I do not claim it is exact, because I have not shown that it can be exact. The word matters as much as the number.

speaker: Aryabhata
where: Konark & the Observatory · The Earth Does Not Stand Still
line: As for notation: we write in words and in a place-value system where each position is ten times the last, and we need a mark for an empty place. Brahmagupta, a century and a bit after me, will write down the arithmetic of that mark and of debts — what you would call negative numbers — including the rule that dividing by it gives nothing usable. Through Baghdad and then al-Andalus, those ten signs become the ones the whole world writes with.

speaker: Mallappa
line: The chariot is three pieces, not one. Look for the joints — they are there if you are honest about it.

speaker: Mallappa
line: Those tank steps are numbered. Cut in one place, assembled in another. A kit of parts.

speaker: Mallappa
line: Strike the pillar gently with your knuckle, not a hammer. Fools with hammers have cost us plenty.

speaker: Nuniz
line: Everyone wants cavalry and nobody here breeds it. That is my entire business model.

speaker: Nuniz
line: I will write all this down when I am home. I will probably exaggerate. Everybody does.

speaker: Nuniz
line: Pepper out, horses in, and a tax at every gate. The gates are where the real kingdom is.

speaker: Hampamma
line: This channel was cut five hundred years ago and it still waters my bananas.

speaker: Hampamma
line: Desilt before the monsoon, not after. Everyone knows and half of them forget.

speaker: Hampamma
line: Empires come and go. The canal has outlasted three of them.

speaker: Abdur Razzaq
line: I am to report whether this kingdom is formidable. You can guess what my report will say.

speaker: Abdur Razzaq
line: Seven circuits of wall, bazaars full of jewels — I will write it exactly as I saw it, and still nobody will believe me.

speaker: Abdur Razzaq
line: An ambassador is a merchant of impressions.

speaker: Allasani Peddana
line: Telugu, Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit in the same hall on the same evening. Nobody thinks it remarkable.

speaker: Allasani Peddana
line: The king writes too — and not badly, which makes him a difficult patron.

speaker: Allasani Peddana
line: They call us the eight elephants. Elephants are slow and remembered. I will take it.

speaker: Mahout Bhima
line: Eleven chambers, one animal each, domed so the heat lifts away from them.

speaker: Mahout Bhima
line: An elephant eats two hundred kilos a day. The stables are an argument about logistics.

speaker: Mahout Bhima
line: Mine knows my voice from fifty paces and ignores it from twenty.

speaker: Dr. Shalini Deshpande
line: Three witnesses to this city. Abdur Razzaq, a Persian envoy in 1443, says he has never seen its like and counts the bazaars. Domingo Paes, a Portuguese horse-trader in the 1520s, says it is as large as Rome and the king’s jewels are beyond counting. And the temple walls, which record grants of land and oil and dancers’ wages. Which do you trust?

speaker: Dr. Shalini Deshpande
line: They are vivid, and vividness is seductive. But ask why each man is writing. Razzaq is an ambassador reporting to a court that wants to know whether this kingdom is formidable. Paes sells horses and writes for people deciding whether to invest. Neither is lying, exactly. Both have a reason to make this place sound enormous.

speaker: Dr. Shalini Deshpande
line: Inscriptions are wonderful and narrow. They tell you precisely what the donor wanted recorded — this much land, this many lamps, this festival — and almost nothing about what the donor wanted hidden. They are dated, which is gold. But a wall full of pious grants will never mention a famine, a defeat or a tax riot.

speaker: Dr. Shalini Deshpande
line: Here is where it gets satisfying. Paes describes irrigation channels; the survey has mapped those channels and some still carry water to Kamalapura’s fields. The inscriptions record the Mahanavami festival; the Dibba platform matches the described procession. Razzaq describes long colonnaded bazaars; we have excavated them in front of the temples. Where all three converge, we are on firm ground. Where they conflict, that is where the interesting question is.

speaker: Dr. Shalini Deshpande
line: Talikota. The later chronicles describe a sudden, total catastrophe — one lost battle, a city stripped in months. The archaeology is messier: burning in some quarters, continuity in others, and Virupaksha temple never stopped being worshipped — there is a priest in it this morning. The abandonment of the capital was real, and it was a process, not a thunderclap. History almost always runs slower than the story about it.

speaker: Amanat Khan
line: The letters grow taller as the panel rises. From the ground they read as one even size. That is the trick.

speaker: Amanat Khan
line: I signed my work. On a building like this, that is either confidence or impertinence.

speaker: Amanat Khan
line: Thuluth script, inlaid in black marble. Measure twice; you cannot un-cut stone.

speaker: Puran
line: Twenty thousand of us, they say, over twenty years. The ledgers have some of our names in them.

speaker: Puran
line: Makrana marble does not yellow and it glows at dusk. That is why we hauled it four hundred kilometres.

speaker: Puran
line: The minarets lean outward a little. Deliberately. If they ever fall, they fall away from the tomb.

speaker: Mirza Nauroz
line: Water runs by gravity from the river, through the channels, into every bed. No pumps anywhere.

speaker: Mirza Nauroz
line: Cypress for death, fruit trees for life, planted in alternation. The garden is an argument.

speaker: Mirza Nauroz
line: Sunken beds, raised walks. You walk at the level of the treetops without noticing.

speaker: Bichitr
line: Persian line, Indian colour, and lately European perspective because the Jesuits brought prints.

speaker: Bichitr
line: Squirrel-hair brushes, down to a single hair for the eyelashes.

speaker: Bichitr
line: I paint the emperor preferring a holy man to a king. He approved it. Think about that.

speaker: Zarina
line: Twenty-eight kinds of stone in one flower. Carnelian, jasper, lapis, jade, turquoise.

speaker: Zarina
line: You cut the recess to fit the stone, not the stone to fit the recess.

speaker: Zarina
line: My grandfather worked on the tomb. My hands do what his hands did.

speaker: Bhishti Ramzan
line: Goatskin on the back, river to the site, all day. Twenty thousand men on this works get thirsty.

speaker: Bhishti Ramzan
line: A bhishti once saved an emperor from drowning and was given the throne for a day. Ask anyone.

speaker: Bhishti Ramzan
line: They will remember the marble. Somebody carried the water that mixed the mortar.

speaker: Jalaluddin Muhammad Akbar
where: Agra & Sikri · The House of Worship
line: Thursday evenings I have them brought in: ulama, Brahmin pandits, Jain munis, Zoroastrian priests, and lately Jesuits from Goa. They argue, and I listen, and they are frequently appalling to one another. I cannot read, as you may know — I have everything read aloud to me. So. How should such a room be governed?

speaker: Jalaluddin Muhammad Akbar
where: Agra & Sikri · The House of Worship
line: Because I rule a country in which most of my subjects do not share my religion, and I intend to rule it for a long time. That is the practical answer. The other answer is that I am curious, and curiosity in a king is cheaper than war. I have remitted the pilgrimage tax, and the jizya on non-Muslims, and I married into Rajput houses whose princes command my armies.

speaker: Jalaluddin Muhammad Akbar
where: Agra & Sikri · The House of Worship
line: Statecraft and conviction are not always enemies.

speaker: Jalaluddin Muhammad Akbar
where: Agra & Sikri · The House of Worship
line: I tried something near that and it went badly. When a king sits in judgement over doctrine, every scholar begins performing for the throne instead of arguing honestly. And the Mahzar of 1579, which gave me authority to decide between conflicting legal opinions, earned me enemies who have not forgiven me yet. Victory in such a room is worth very little.

speaker: Jalaluddin Muhammad Akbar
where: Agra & Sikri · The House of Worship
line: Loudly. Abdul Qadir Badauni sat in my own court writing a history that calls me a heretic — and I kept him employed, translating the Mahabharata into Persian. That is the Razmnama, and it is one of the things I am proudest of. A library where only one kind of book is allowed is a storeroom, not a library.

speaker: Jalaluddin Muhammad Akbar
where: Agra & Sikri · The House of Worship
line: The Ramayana, the Atharva Veda, the Yoga Vasistha, Lilavati for the mathematics, the Panchatantra. Abu’l Fazl has compiled the Ain-i-Akbari — revenue, ranks, customs, crop prices, the whole machinery written down. And the painters have mixed Persian line with Indian colour until the result is neither and both. Basawan, Daswanth, and later Mansur, who paints birds so exactly that naturalists still use him.

speaker: Jalaluddin Muhammad Akbar
where: Agra & Sikri · The House of Worship
line: Then let that be the rule, and let it be called sulh-i-kul — peace with all. Each may expound; none may revile. And let me be honest about the limits, since you seem to want honesty: this is my court’s policy, not a constitution. My great-grandson Aurangzeb will reimpose the jizya. A tolerance that depends on the character of one ruler is only ever on loan. Whatever you build, build it so it does not need a good king.

speaker: Tanaji
line: Give me sixty men who grew up on this ridge over six hundred who did not.

speaker: Tanaji
line: We climb at night. Ropes, bare feet, no lamps. The wall is only as strong as the hour it is watched.

speaker: Tanaji
line: They ask how many we are. The honest answer is: fewer than you, and in better places.

speaker: Sakhubai
line: Count the cisterns, not the cannon. A fort falls when the water runs out, not when the wall cracks.

speaker: Sakhubai
line: Cut into living rock, roofed against the sun, filled by the monsoon. A year’s supply if nobody is wasteful.

speaker: Sakhubai
line: Every siege story is really a story about water.

speaker: Ahilyabai Holkar
line: Battles are remembered. Wells are used. I would rather be useful.

speaker: Ahilyabai Holkar
line: Ghats at Varanasi, the temple at Somnath, roads for pilgrims, rest-houses. Stone outlives armies.

speaker: Ahilyabai Holkar
line: They call me a widow queen as though it were a limitation. I have thirty years of accounts that say otherwise.

speaker: Yesaji
line: Every ridge between here and the coast, and which of them you can cross in the rains.

speaker: Yesaji
line: The enemy has maps. We have the actual hills. It is not the same advantage.

speaker: Yesaji
line: Walk at night, sleep at noon. The heat is a sentry working for us.

speaker: Sakharam
line: Light armour, light blades. If a man cannot run up this path in it, I have failed.

speaker: Sakharam
line: The pata, the dandpatta — a gauntlet sword. Vicious in a corridor, useless on a plain.

speaker: Sakharam
line: We repair more than we forge. A campaign is mostly mending.

speaker: Rani Padmini’s herald
line: Mewar fought the same arithmetic two centuries earlier: few men, high ground, long patience.

speaker: Rani Padmini’s herald
line: The bards sing the sieges. The chronicles on the other side sing the victories. Read both.

speaker: Rani Padmini’s herald
line: Chittorgarh is two hundred and eighty hectares of plateau. You do not take it in an afternoon.

speaker: Balaji
line: Measured, assessed, receipted. If a soldier takes grain without a receipt he answers for it.

speaker: Balaji
line: Chauth is a share, not a sack. The difference is the whole character of the state.

speaker: Balaji
line: Records in Marathi now. My father wrote them in Persian and could not read them aloud to a farmer.

speaker: Shivaji Bhonsle
line: Every envoy who comes up this hill asks me the same thing: why do I not meet the imperial army in the open field, as a king should? They have forty thousand horse and artillery trains and more money than I will ever see. Tell me what you would have me do with my light cavalry and my four hundred ridges.

speaker: Shivaji Bhonsle
line: Legitimacy is what you have left after you survive. An army that fights only where the enemy is strongest is not honourable; it is obliging. And I have not avoided fighting — ask at Pratapgad, ask at Sinhagad. I avoid fighting on ground chosen by someone else. There is a difference, and it is the whole difference.

speaker: Shivaji Bhonsle
line: We call it ganimi kava. Move at night, strike the baggage and the paymaster, never the armoured centre. Hold the passes, let the monsoon do half the work — their cavalry and guns sink in the ghats from June to September while my infantry walks. The Mawal men know every goat track on these ridges because they were born on them. That is not a tactic. That is a home.

speaker: Shivaji Bhonsle
line: A single fort is a trap. Three hundred forts within signalling distance are a system — lose one and the garrison walks to the next. Water decides everything: cisterns cut into the rock, enough for a year. Gates turned at right angles so no elephant can build momentum. Bastions placed to shoot along the wall, not out from it. Torna was the first I took, at sixteen. Raigad is where I was crowned.

speaker: Shivaji Bhonsle
line: Which is exactly why I built one. The Siddis sit at Janjira, the Portuguese at Goa, the English at Bombay, and every one of them can land where they please while the land powers watch. So: Sindhudurg and Vijaydurg on the rocks, cruisers to escort our own merchants, and a Sarkhel to command them. Later Kanhoji Angre will hold this coast against three European navies at once. A kingdom with a coast and no fleet has a door with no latch.

speaker: Shivaji Bhonsle
line: Eight ministers — the Ashta Pradhan. Peshwa for administration, Amatya for accounts, Sachiv for correspondence, Mantri for intelligence, Senapati for the army, Sumant for foreign affairs, Nyayadhish for justice, Panditrao for religious endowments. Offices, not hereditary gifts — that was the intention, though my successors did not keep to it. I also had the court records put into Marathi and Sanskrit instead of Persian.

speaker: Shivaji Bhonsle
line: By taxing, not looting — and I am strict about this. Chauth and sardeshmukhi are assessed shares, collected on a measurement of the land, with written receipts. My orders to my own commanders forbid touching the standing crop, the cattle or the women of a village, and I have had officers punished for it. A soldier who burns a village has destroyed next year’s revenue to feed himself today. That is not ferocity. That is arithmetic.

speaker: Ekarupa
line: Let me finish the scroll. One story, one voice, no more work for you. You have been so careful. Aren’t you tired? I will make my claims. You may answer them, or you may simply agree. Agreeing is so much easier.

speaker: Maitri
line: It was never a villain, you know. It is the part of every listener that wants it simple, and that includes me, and that includes you. We do not beat it. We check it, every time. Look at the cords now.

speaker: Maitri
line: Namaste, Gathak. I am Maitri, keeper of the Gatha. If you can hear this, the voices are working.
